Use the spread operator to: (1) create a copy of the prices array, (2) add 9500 to the end of the copy without mutating the original, (3) merge the original with a second array [2500, 3700], (4) log the original length (should be unchanged) and the merged array.
What is the difference between the spread operator (`...`) and the rest operator (`...`)? They look identical — how does JavaScript know which one you mean?
questions.sample_answer: Both use the `...` syntax but serve opposite purposes. The context determines which one JavaScript uses: Spread EXPANDS an iterable into individual elements — used in function calls (`Math.max(...nums)`), array literals (`[...arr, newItem]`), and object literals (`{...obj, newProp}`). It takes one thing and expands it into many. Rest COLLECTS multiple individual elements into one array — used in function parameters (`function sum(...nums)`) and destructuring (`const [first, ...rest] = arr`). It takes many things and packs them into one. JavaScript knows by position: in a function definition's parameter list or on the left side of a destructuring assignment, `...` is rest (collecting). Everywhere else (right side of assignment, inside array/object literals, in function call arguments), `...` is spread (expanding).

Use the spread operator on objects to create a new `updatedProduct` from the product below. Add a `discount` property of 10 and override the `price` to 4050 (10% off). Log both the original price and the updated price to prove the original wasn't mutated.
When using spread to copy an object (`{...obj}`), is it a deep copy or a shallow copy? What problem does this cause with nested objects?
questions.sample_answer: Spread creates a SHALLOW copy — only the top-level properties are copied. Nested objects and arrays are NOT cloned; they're shared references between the original and the copy. Problem: if you do `const copy = {...user}` and user has `address: {city: 'Lagos'}`, then `copy.address === user.address` (same reference). Mutating `copy.address.city = 'Abuja'` also changes `user.address.city` because both point to the same address object. This breaks the immutability guarantee for nested data. Solutions: (1) manually spread nested objects too: `{...user, address: {...user.address, city: 'Abuja'}}`, (2) use `structuredClone(obj)` for a true deep copy, (3) use JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) for simple objects (doesn't handle functions or special types).

Use destructuring in a map callback to add a `passed` property to each student. Then use destructuring in a filter callback to keep only those where `passed` is true. Log the filtered names.
What is destructuring in function parameters? How does `function greet({name, age})` differ from `function greet(person)`? Give an advantage of each approach.
questions.sample_answer: Destructuring in parameters extracts properties from the argument directly in the function signature. `function greet({name, age})` pulls name and age out of the passed object — inside the function you use `name` and `age` directly. `function greet(person)` receives the whole object — inside you use `person.name` and `person.age`. Advantage of destructuring: cleaner code inside the function (no repeated `person.` prefix), self-documenting signature (you can see exactly which properties the function uses), works well in map/filter callbacks (`students.filter(({score}) => score >= 50)`). Advantage of the whole object: you have access to ALL properties without listing them; you can pass the object to other functions; you can iterate its properties with Object.keys; and the function can work with objects of different shapes.

Write a function `mergeSettings(defaults, ...overrides)` that uses the spread operator to merge all override objects into the defaults, with later overrides taking precedence. Call it with a defaults object and two override objects. Log the final merged result.
What are default parameters and why are they useful? How do they compare to the old pattern of `value = value || defaultValue` inside the function body?
questions.sample_answer: Default parameters provide a fallback value directly in the function signature: `function greet(name = 'World')`. If the argument is undefined (not passed or explicitly undefined), the default is used. They're useful because: (1) the intent is clear from the signature — you see the defaults immediately, (2) they work correctly with all falsy values. The old pattern `value = value || defaultValue` has a bug: it triggers the default for ANY falsy value — 0, '', false, null — not just undefined. If `fontSize` should default to 14 but the user passes 0 (valid!), `fontSize || 14` gives 14 (wrong). Default parameters only activate for undefined, so `fontSize = 14` with argument 0 correctly gives 0. Default params are also self-documenting in IDE tooltips and documentation generators.

Why is immutability important in modern JavaScript? How do spread and destructuring help achieve immutable updates? Give a practical scenario where mutation causes a bug.
questions.sample_answer: Immutability means never modifying existing data — instead, creating new copies with changes. It's important because: (1) predictability — you know data hasn't changed unexpectedly, (2) debugging — you can compare before/after states, (3) frameworks like React require it for change detection (React doesn't re-render if you mutate state directly). Spread helps by creating new arrays/objects: `{...user, name: 'New'}` creates a new object instead of modifying user. Destructuring helps by extracting values for transformation without touching the source. Bug scenario: You have a user list displayed in a table. You sort the array with `.sort()` (which mutates). The original reference in state is now also sorted — React doesn't detect a change (same reference), so the UI doesn't update. With `[...users].sort()`, you get a new sorted array, the reference changes, React detects it, and the UI updates correctly.
